## Overview

`mgrcli` is the command-line companion to the MOFography Python API. It wraps the
same Rust-accelerated pipeline (`dgrid_from_atoms_rust` → `do_periodic_segmentation_rust`
→ downstream analysis) so you can analyze one or many CIFs without writing any
Python.

The main entry is `mgrcli process`:

```bash
mgrcli process <cifs...> [flags]
```

A single invocation can produce:

- **Per-CIF `*_results.npz`** — the same segmentation dict you'd get from the
  Python API (dgrid, maxima, regions, connections, RAG-as-arrays).
- **Pore-diameter CSV** with LCD, PLD, DFSD, and percolation history (with `--pore-dia`).
- **PSD CSVs** — uniform, pocketwise, and accessible variants (with `--psd`,
  `--psd-accessible`).
- **Surface-area and void-volume CSVs + Plotly bar charts** (with `--sa` / `--vol`).
- **RAG pickle** — a NetworkX graph of the pore network (with `--rag`).
- **Pocket types** — `env_cluster` multi-modal fingerprints (with `--types`).
- **HTML visualizations** — Plotly or Three.js (with `--plot-html`).

This tutorial walks through installation, the canonical command, every key
flag, the output layout, and how to drop down to the Python API when the
CLI is not enough.

## Prerequisites

- A working MOFography environment (see the [Installation](install.qmd) guide).
- A CIF file. The tutorials use `docs/IRMOF-1.cif` from this repo.
- About 5–10 seconds per CIF on a modern laptop for the canonical flags
  (`--pore-dia --psd --rag --types` on IRMOF-1 takes ~4 s end-to-end on M-series).

## Installation

### From PyPI (recommended)

```bash
pip install mgrcli
```

This pulls in `mgrcli` plus its pinned runtime dependencies
(`ase`, `pymatgen`, `plotly`, `scikit-image`, `networkx`, …) and the prebuilt
Rust extension for your platform.

### From source (editable)

If you want to hack on the CLI or pin a development branch:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/arung-northwestern/mgr_cli_py.git
cd mgr_cli_py/python_cli
pip install -e .
```

`pip install -e .` picks up your local edits to `mgrcli/cli.py` without a
reinstall.

### Sanity check

```bash
mgrcli --version     # prints the package version
mgrcli --help        # top-level subcommand list
```

In a Python notebook, you can also confirm the binary is on `PATH` and report
its version:

```{python}
import shutil, subprocess
print("mgrcli on PATH:", shutil.which("mgrcli"))
print(subprocess.run(["mgrcli", "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
```

## The canonical command

For most MOFs — IRMOF-1, UiO-66, ZIF-8, HKUST-1 — this one command is
all you need to get the full pore-network picture:

```bash
mgrcli process IRMOF-1.cif \
  --dgrid-method rust_exact \
  --vdw-radii-set bondi \
  --b rust_det \
  --pore-dia \
  --psd \
  --rag
```

It:

1. Computes the **distance grid** with the thread-parallel `rust_exact`
   backend (default-correct for all cell types).
2. Runs **periodic segmentation** with the deterministic `rust_det`
   watershed.
3. Adds **pore-diameter analysis** (LCD, PLD, DFSD + percolation history).
4. Adds the **PSD** (uniform + pocketwise probe sampling).
5. Saves the **RAG** as a pickle for downstream graph work.

Add `--types` to also detect pocket-type families via `env_cluster`:

```bash
mgrcli process IRMOF-1.cif \
  --dgrid-method rust_exact --vdw-radii-set bondi --b rust_det \
  --pore-dia --psd --rag --types
```

This is the command to copy-paste for a "one-shot full analysis".

## End-to-end smoke test

Run the canonical command from inside this docs folder. The output lands in
`hts_output/IRMOF-1/` (the convention used by the Streamlit HTS tab — any
directory you pass to `-o` works, but `hts_output/<stem>/` is the standard
layout for batch HTS runs).

```{python}
import os, subprocess, shutil, pathlib
from pathlib import Path

os.chdir(Path("/Users/arungopalan/repos/mofography/docs"))

out_dir = Path("hts_output/IRMOF-1")
if out_dir.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(out_dir)

result = subprocess.run(
    [
        "mgrcli", "process", "IRMOF-1.cif",
        "-o", str(out_dir),
        "--dgrid-method", "rust_exact",
        "--vdw-radii-set", "bondi",
        "--b", "rust_det",
        "--pore-dia", "--psd", "--rag", "--types",
        "--disable-tqdm",
    ],
    capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300,
)
print("returncode:", result.returncode)
print("--- stdout (tail) ---")
print("\n".join(result.stdout.splitlines()[-20:]))
if result.returncode != 0:
    print("--- stderr (tail) ---")
    print("\n".join(result.stderr.splitlines()[-20:]))
```

The expected return code is `0`; the tail of stdout should show the per-region
PSD stats, the env_cluster type count, and the final `Results saved to: ..._results.npz` line.

## Output directory structure

After the smoke test, `hts_output/IRMOF-1/` contains:

```{python}
for p in sorted(out_dir.iterdir()):
    print(f"{p.stat().st_size:>9,d}  {p.name}")
```

| File pattern | Produced by | Contents |
|--------------|-------------|----------|
| `IRMOF-1_results.npz` | always | Compressed NumPy archive with dgrid, maxima, regions, regions_pbc, unique_regions, connections, pocket typing, etc. — the same dict shape returned by the Python API. |
| `IRMOF-1_pore_dia.csv` | `--pore-dia` | `LCD`, `PLD`, `DFSD` in Å + the percolation history point count. |
| `IRMOF-1_psd_psd_uniform.csv` | `--psd` | Globally sampled pore-size distribution (the doubled `psd_psd` is intentional — `save_psd_csv` always appends `_psd_uniform` / `_psd_pockets` to its base). |
| `IRMOF-1_psd_psd_pockets.csv` | `--psd` | Per-pocket probe-occupiable PSDs. |
| `IRMOF-1_psd_accessible_psd_uniform.csv` | `--psd-accessible` | PSD restricted to the percolating cluster at `--probe-radius`. |
| `IRMOF-1_psd_accessible_psd_pockets.csv` | `--psd-accessible` | Same, per pocket. |
| `IRMOF-1_sa_surface_area.csv` | `--sa` | Surface-area breakdown (geometric / accessible / framework-touching). |
| `IRMOF-1_vol_void_volume.csv` | `--vol` | Void-volume breakdown. |
| `IRMOF-1_surface_area_plot.html` | `--sa` + `--sa-plot-html` | Plotly bar chart of SA components. |
| `IRMOF-1_void_volume_plot.html` | `--vol` + `--vol-plot-html` | Plotly bar chart of volume components. |
| `IRMOF-1_rag_clustered.pkl` | `--rag` or `--types` | Pickled NetworkX region-adjacency graph; load with `pickle.load` / `networkx.readwrite.read_gpickle`. |
| `IRMOF-1.html` | `--plot-html` | Standalone 3D visualization of the segmentation (Plotly or Three.js). |
| `IRMOF-1_percolation.html` | `--percolation-plot` | Percolation cluster growth, useful for sanity-checking the LCD/PLD. |

```{python}
import pandas as pd
print("--- IRMOF-1_pore_dia.csv ---")
print(pd.read_csv(out_dir / "IRMOF-1_pore_dia.csv").to_string(index=False))
```

## Reading the .npz back in Python

The CLI saves a compressed NumPy archive so you can mix batch CLI runs with
custom Python post-processing without re-running segmentation.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# The CLI's results .npz contains object arrays (connections, pocket_type_summary,
# mat_atoms, ...), so allow_pickle=True is required.
with np.load(out_dir / "IRMOF-1_results.npz", allow_pickle=True) as z:
    print("keys:", sorted(z.files))
    print(f"  dgrid shape:           {z['dgrid'].shape}")
    print(f"  regions_pbc shape:     {z['regions_pbc'].shape}")
    print(f"  n maxima (pbc):        {len(z['maxima_pbc'])}")
    conns = z['connections']
    # Stored as a 0-d object array — .item() unpacks the inner Python list
    conn_list = conns.item() if conns.dtype == object and conns.shape == () else conns
    print(f"  n connections:         {len(conn_list)}")
    if 'pocket_type_summary' in z.files:
        summary = z['pocket_type_summary']
        # Stored as a 0-d object array containing a Python list[dict]
        if summary.dtype == object and summary.shape == ():
            summary = summary.item()
        print(f"  n pocket types:        {len(summary)}")
        for t in summary:
            print(f"    type {t['type_id']}: n={t['n_pockets']}, "
                  f"max_r ∈ [{t['max_r_min_a']:.2f}, {t['max_r_max_a']:.2f}] Å, "
                  f"vol ∈ [{t['volume_min_a3']:.0f}, {t['volume_max_a3']:.0f}] Å³")
```

> For richer, typed Python access (e.g. the `PocketTypingResult` object
> with `.n_types`, `.type_summary`, `.rep_to_type`), use the Python API —
> see [Pocket Type Detection](pockets_detection.qmd) and the
> [CLI → Python workflow section](#when-to-drop-down-to-the-python-api) below.

## Key flags reference

The `process` subcommand has ~30 flags. They split into five groups:
**input/output**, **analysis parameters**, **boolean flags**, **analysis
options**, and **visualization**. The defaults mirror the Streamlit web app
so a CLI run produces the same numbers as a click-through on the site.

### Distance-grid method (`--dgrid-method`)

| Value | Backend | When to use |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `rust_exact` | Thread-parallel Rust, voxel-exact | **Default.** Correct for all cell types, including non-orthorhombic. |
| `rust_aabb` | R-tree accelerated | Large unit cells; trades a small approximation for ~2-5× less RAM. See [Distance Grid tutorial](distance_grid.qmd). |
| `rust_aabb_interp` | Coarse R-tree + trilinear interp | Very large cells where even `rust_aabb` is heavy. |
| `python_aabb` | Pure-Python AABB | Slowest; use only for parity checks against the Python API. |

> **Do not** use the deprecated `dgrid_from_atoms_gpu` or
> `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb` paths — they mis-handle non-orthorhombic
> cells. The `*_rust` backends are the only correct path on skewed cells.

Tuning knobs for the AABB backends:

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|------|---------|--------|
| `--dgrid-block-size` | 50000 | Voxels per block for `python_aabb`. Lower = less RAM, more Python overhead. |
| `--dgrid-n-neighbors` | 10 | R-tree neighbor count for `rust_aabb` / `rust_aabb_interp`. Higher = more accurate, slower. |
| `--dgrid-coarse-factor` | 2 | Coarsening factor for `rust_aabb_interp` only. Higher = much faster, coarser approximation. |

For most MOFs the auto policy is fine: by default `mgrcli` will
**auto-switch from `rust_exact` to `rust_aabb` for very large cells**.
Pass `--no-auto-dgrid` to disable that policy and stay on `rust_exact`.

### Watershed backend (`-b` / `--backend` / `--watershed-backend`)

| Value | Backend | When to use |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `rust_det` | Deterministic Rust watershed | **Default.** Deterministic, fast, matches the web app. |
| `rust_det_parallel` | Same algorithm, parallelized | Larger cells where serial `rust_det` is the bottleneck. |
| `rust_bucket` | Rust 0-arg bucket queue | Legacy. Faster on some inputs but the basin order can differ — keep `rust_det` for reproducibility. |
| `skimage` | scikit-image `watershed` | Pure-Python; only useful as a cross-check. Requires `scikit-image`. |

### VDW radii set (`--vdw-radii-set`)

| Value | Source | Notes |
|-------|--------|-------|
| `bondi` | Bondi (1964) | **Default.** Matches the web app and the validated canonical workflow. |
| `crc` | CRC Handbook | Slightly smaller radii on metals; can change pocket-typing band counts. |
| `alvarez` | Alvarez (2018) | Heavier on metals; recommended when probing open-metal sites. |

See [VDW Radii Comparison](vdw_radii_comparison.md) for the full
sensitivity study.

### Surface area integration (`--sa-method`)

| Value | Algorithm |
|-------|-----------|
| `mc` (default) | Monte Carlo shell sampling. Fast, accurate; same as web app. |
| `mesh` | Marching-cubes surface area. Slower; closer to `pymatgen`-style estimates. |

### Accessibility method (`--accessibility-method`, `--lattice-variant`)

Drives the percolation test that decides which pockets are reachable from
outside the unit cell:

| Value | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| `winding` (default) | Winding-number percolation. Fast, robust, matches web app. |
| `lattice` | Lattice-based percolation. `--lattice-variant` chooses `v1` (older) or `v2` (newer, default). |

Accessibility applies to `--pore-dia`, `--sa`, and `--vol`. Combine with
`--no-window-fp` to disable the window-fingerprint rescue for accessible
SA / vol (only meaningful with `winding`).

### Segmentation parameters

These map 1:1 to the Python API parameters of `do_periodic_segmentation_rust`:

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|------|---------|--------|
| `-s`, `--spacing` | 0.5 Å | Grid resolution. Halve → 8× more voxels; the single most expensive knob. |
| `-H`, `--h` | 0.2 Å | H-maxima persistence. Higher = fewer, larger pockets. |
| `-mt`, `--mask-thickness` | 0.05 Å | Void-space threshold. Increase to merge nearby pockets. |
| `-ta`, `--threshold-abs` | 1.5 Å | Maxima must be at least this far from the framework. |
| `-md`, `--min-distance` | 1.5 Å | Minimum separation between distinct maxima. |
| `-ms`, `--minimum-window-separation` | 1.0 Å | Minimum separation between detected windows. |
| `-wt`, `--wall-thickness` | 0.05 | Wall-thickness fraction for window detection. |
| `-ep`, `--extra-padding` | 5.0 Å | Extra PBC padding beyond the +5 Å default. |
| `-mrs`, `--min-region-size` | 0.001 | Filter regions smaller than this fraction of the padded grid. |

> **Heads up:** the legacy "batch" profile used `mask_thickness=0.5` and
> `rust_bucket` (see `mgrcli generate-config --profile legacy`). The web /
> default profile is the validated one for pocket typing — keep it unless
> you have a specific reason to regress.

### Probe radius

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|------|---------|--------|
| `--probe-radius` | 1.2 Å (He) | Probe for surface area, void volume, and accessible PSD. |
| `--probe-radius-psd` | 1.2 Å | Probe for the pocket PSD used in `env_cluster` typing. |

### Pocket typing (`--types` / `--pocket-typing`)

| Value | Algorithm |
|-------|-----------|
| `env_cluster` (default with `--types`) | Multi-modal fingerprinting: pocket PSD + framework SH + connectivity SH. The validated, recommended method. |
| `legacy_js` | Older RAG + Jensen-Shannon divergence clustering. Kept for regression; less stable. |
| `none` (default without `--types`) | Skip typing — just save the RAG. |

`--types` is a shorthand for `--pocket-typing env_cluster`. It always saves
the RAG pickle (`<stem>_rag_clustered.pkl`) in addition to running the
typing pass.

### Boolean flags

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--no-connections` | Skip window + connection detection. Faster, but you lose the pore graph. |
| `--no-auto-dgrid` | Disable auto-switch from `rust_exact` → `rust_aabb` for large cells. |
| `--no-window-fp` | Disable window-fingerprint rescue for accessible SA / vol (winding). |
| `--return-padded-regions` | Include the padded region array in the .npz (default off). |
| `--return-dgrid` | Keep dgrid in the .npz (default on). |
| `--disable-tqdm` | Suppress progress bars (good for log files). |
| `--plot-html` | Save a standalone 3D HTML viewer after processing. |
| `--no-stylize` | Disable stylized framework rendering in plots. |
| `--pore-dia` | Compute LCD/PLD/DFSD + percolation history. |
| `--percolation-plot` | Save `<stem>_percolation.html` (cluster growth). |
| `--sa-plot-html` | Save `<stem>_surface_area_plot.html`. |
| `--vol-plot-html` | Save `<stem>_void_volume_plot.html`. |
| `--psd` | Compute pore size distribution. |
| `--psd-accessible` | Compute accessible (percolation-filtered) PSD at `--probe-radius`. |
| `--sa` | Compute surface area. |
| `--vol` | Compute void volume. |
| `--auto-params` | Auto-estimate optimal parameters from the cell geometry. |
| `--types` | Detect pocket types via `env_cluster`. |
| `--rag` | Save the RAG pickle (no typing). |
| `--theme {dark,white}` | Plot theme (default `dark`). |

### Visualization backends

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|------|---------|--------|
| `--plot-html` | off | Save `<stem>.html` viewer. |
| `--plot-backend {plotly,threejs}` | `plotly` | Viewer engine. Three.js exports smaller, more portable HTML. |
| `--percolation-plot-backend {plotly,threejs}` | `threejs` | Percolation plot engine. |
| `--html-dir` | same as `-o` | Separate folder for HTML outputs. |

## Re-running from a saved config

If you've been clicking around the web app and want to capture the exact
parameter set as a JSON config:

```bash
mgrcli generate-config -o my_run.json
# edit my_run.json …
mgrcli process IRMOF-1.cif -c my_run.json
```

`generate-config` writes a config matching the current defaults (web
profile by default; `--profile legacy` for the older batch defaults). The
process subcommand accepts it via `-c/--config`.

## Processing many CIFs

The positional argument is variadic — pass as many CIFs as you like:

```bash
mgrcli process mofs/*.cif -o ./results/ --pore-dia --psd --rag --disable-tqdm
```

Each CIF is processed in turn; outputs are prefixed with the CIF stem
(`<stem>_results.npz`, `<stem>_pore_dia.csv`, …). Failed CIFs are
logged and skipped — a single bad file does not abort the run.

## Plotting an existing .npz

If you already saved a `*_results.npz` (via the CLI or the Python API) and
want to (re)render its HTML viewer:

```bash
mgrcli plot IRMOF-1_results.npz -o ./plots/ --plot-backend threejs --theme dark
```

`plot` reads the .npz, attaches a `.html` viewer with the same name stem
into the output directory, and respects the same `--plot-backend` /
`--theme` / `--no-stylize` / `--surface-taubin-intensity` knobs as
`--plot-html` on `process`.

## Launching the web app

If you'd rather click through, `mgrcli interactive` boots the same
Streamlit app you can use locally:

```bash
mgrcli interactive             # default port
mgrcli interactive --port 8501 # specific port
mgrcli interactive --clean     # kill stale Streamlit processes first
```

`interactive` is the same backend as the deployed Hugging Face Space; the
CLI just removes the need to clone + install the Streamlit code by hand.

## When to drop down to the Python API

The CLI is the right tool for:

- **One-shot analysis** of a handful of MOFs.
- **Batch HTS-style runs** on hundreds to thousands of CIFs.
- **Capturing reproducible parameter sets** in a JSON config.
- Producing **standardized artifacts** (`.npz` + CSVs) for downstream
  pipelines.

But the Python API is strictly more flexible. Drop down to Python when you need:

- **Custom post-processing** on the segmentation dict
  (`dgrid`, `regions_pbc`, `connections`, `pbc_groups`).
- **Typed `PocketTypingResult`** with `.n_types`, `.n_pockets`,
  `.type_summary`, `.rep_to_type`, `.regions_cluster`
  (see [Pocket Type Detection](pockets_detection.qmd)).
- **Custom visualizations** (e.g. `show_mof_plotly(seg, atoms, typed_result=...)`).
- **Tighter integration** with Dask, MOFDB, or PoroNet pipelines
  (see [HTS Dask](hts_using_mofography.ipynb) and the
  [PoroNet tutorial](PoroNet.qmd)).
- **Access to `close_or_inside_maxima`** (voxel coords of pockets' interior
  maxima) or other low-level arrays the CLI does not surface.

The handoff is clean: every artifact the CLI writes is also a valid input
to the Python API. You can read the .npz with `numpy.load`, or just
re-load the CIF and re-run a single step from the CLI's
`compute_*` functions (they are importable from `mgrcli.cli`).

## Tips

- **Start with the canonical command**, then add flags. Defaults mirror
  the web app and are validated against IRMOF-1, UiO-66, ZIF-8, HKUST-1,
  NU-1000, and ZIF-20.
- **Use `-o hts_output/<stem>/`** so the per-CIF artifacts live in a
  predictable folder layout — that's what the Streamlit HTS tab expects.
- **Reproducibility:** pair `-c my_run.json` with `--disable-tqdm` for
  clean logs you can diff between runs.
- **For very large cells**, the default auto-AABB policy already switches
  to `rust_aabb` — you only need to override `--dgrid-method` if you want
  to force one specific backend.
- **VDW sensitivity:** if pocket-type counts look wrong, re-run with
  `--vdw-radii-set bondi` and compare against `crc` / `alvarez`. See the
  [VDW Sensitivity Problem](pocket-typing-radii-sensitivity-problem.md)
  deep dive.
- **The CLI hides nothing the API exposes** — every artifact on disk is
  also reachable from Python. The `*_results.npz` is the canonical
  handoff.
